claim: Huntington's disease (HD) is a dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorder typically manifesting in midlife with motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms, leading to death after 15–20 years.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is a dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorder typically manifesting in midlife with motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms, leading to death after 15–20 years (Vonsattel et al., 1985; Harper, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vonsattel et al., 1985 and Harper, 1999

claim: HD is caused by the inheritance of an expansion >35 repeats of a polymorphic CAG repeat tract in the HTT gene.
source: HD is caused by the inheritance of an expansion >35 repeats of a polymorphic CAG repeat tract in the HTT gene (Macdonald et al., 1993)
evidence: Supported by citation to Macdonald et al., 1993

claim: Medium-spiny neurons (MSNs) of the striatum are exquisitely sensitive to the HD mutation.
source: ultimately resulting in cellular dysfunction and death, with medium-spiny neurons (MSNs) of the striatum being exquisitely sensitive to this mutation (Vonsattel et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vonsattel et al., 1985

claim: The expanded HTT CAG repeat undergoes further time-dependent, CAG length-dependent and tissue/cell-type-dependent expansion.
source: The expanded HTT CAG repeat undergoes further time-dependent, CAG length-dependent and tissue/cell-type-dependent expansion (Wheeler et al., 1999; Kennedy and Shelbourne, 2000; Kennedy et al., 2003; Veitch et al., 2007; Gonitel et al., 2008; Swami et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2011; Kovalenko et al., 2012; Larson et al., 2015; Geraerts et al., 2016; Ament et al., 2017; Mouro Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The HTT CAG repeat is highly unstable in the brain, particularly in MSNs.
source: The repeat is highly unstable in the brain, particularly in MSNs (Kovalenko et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kovalenko et al., 2012

claim: Individual-specific differences in the extent of somatic CAG expansion in HD postmortem brain are associated with age of onset.
source: with individual-specific differences in the extent of somatic CAG expansion in HD postmortem brain associated with age of onset (Swami et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swami et al., 2009

claim: Recent genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for modifiers of HD onset highlight somatic CAG expansion as a key driver of the rate of disease onset.
source: Recent genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for modifiers of HD onset highlight somatic CAG expansion as a key driver of the rate of disease onset (Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's Disease (GeM-HD) Consortium, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to GeM-HD Consortium, 2019

claim: Genetic data from GWAS and extensive cross-tissue analyses of somatic instability support a two-step model of HD pathogenesis whereby cellular vulnerability is determined by both the rate of somatic CAG expansion and a toxic process(es) triggered by somatically expanded repeats.
source: Genetic data from these GWAS as well as extensive cross-tissue analyses of somatic instability (Mouro Pinto et al., 2020) support a two-step model of HD pathogenesis whereby cellular vulnerability is determined by both the rate of somatic CAG expansion and a toxic process(es) triggered by somatically expanded repeats.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mouro Pinto et al., 2020 and inference from GWAS data

claim: Several DNA repair genes modify somatic CAG expansion in HD mouse models, with mismatch repair (MMR) genes being critical drivers of this process.
source: Several DNA repair genes modify somatic CAG expansion in HD mouse models, with mismatch repair (MMR) genes being critical drivers of this process. (Wheeler et al., 2003; Dragileva et al., 2009; Tomé et al., 2013; Pinto et al., 2013; Kovtun et al., 2007; Mollersen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Local chromatin structure has been suggested to influence repeat instability.
source: For example, local chromatin structure has been suggested to influence repeat instability (Gorbunova et al., 2004; Jung and Bonini, 2007; Libby et al., 2003; Libby et al., 2008; Dion et al., 2008; Yang and Freudenreich, 2010; Nestor and Monckton, 2011; Neto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Global transcriptional dysregulation and epigenetic alterations have emerged as likely significant contributors to HD disease pathogenesis.
source: However, global transcriptional dysregulation and epigenetic alterations have emerged as likely significant contributors to disease pathogenesis (Glajch and Sadri-Vakili, 2015; Sharma and Taliyan, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glajch and Sadri-Vakili, 2015 and Sharma and Taliyan, 2015

claim: Several studies have shown beneficial effects of HDAC inhibitors in HD mouse models.
source: There is an extensive history of investigating histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors in HD and several studies have shown beneficial effects in HD mouse models (Hockly et al., 2003; Gardian et al., 2005; Thomas et al., 2008; Mielcarek et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2012a; Jia et al., 2012b; Jia et al., 2016; Chopra et al., 2016; Suelves et al., 2017; Siebzehnrübl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: A selective HDAC3 inhibitor reduced CAG expansion in HD mice.
source: Interestingly one study found that a selective HDAC3 inhibitor also reduced CAG expansion in HD mice (Suelves et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suelves et al., 2017

claim: HDAC2 or HDAC3 protein are no longer detectable in the majority of the striatal cells in Hdac2 KO or Hdac3 KO mice.
source: HDAC2 or HDAC3 protein are no longer detectable in the majority of the striatal cells in Hdac2 KO or Hdac3 KO mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The remaining HDAC2- or HDAC3-immunopositive cells in Hdac2 KO or Hdac3 KO mice are DARPP-32 negative, reflecting continued expression in cell types other than MSNs in the striatum.
source: The remaining HDAC2- or HDAC3-immunopositive cells are DARPP-32 negative, reflecting continued expression in cell types other than MSNs in the striatum (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Western blots confirmed the loss of HDAC2 protein in striata from Hdac2 KO mice.
source: Western blots also confirmed the loss of HDAC2 protein in striata from Hdac2 KO mice and revealed a compensatory increase in HDAC1 protein levels as seen in other systems with long-term loss of HDAC2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Hdac2 KO mice revealed a compensatory increase in HDAC1 protein levels.
source: Western blots also confirmed the loss of HDAC2 protein in striata from Hdac2 KO mice and revealed a compensatory increase in HDAC1 protein levels as seen in other systems with long-term loss of HDAC2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: HDAC2 and HDAC3 expression were not altered in the cortex of Hdac2 KO or Hdac3 KO mice.
source: As expected, HDAC2 and HDAC3 expression were not altered in the cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Hdac2 KO mice appeared indistinguishable from their littermates.
source: Whereas Hdac2 ΚO mice appeared indistinguishable from their littermates, Hdac3 ΚO mice were significantly smaller in size and had lower body weight
evidence: Based on observation of mice

claim: Hdac3 KO mice were significantly smaller in size and had lower body weight.
source: Whereas Hdac2 ΚO mice appeared indistinguishable from their littermates, Hdac3 ΚO mice were significantly smaller in size and had lower body weight
evidence: Based on observation of mice

claim: More than half of the total number of Hdac3 KO pups did not survive to five months of age.
source: with more than half of the total number of Hdac3 ΚO pups not surviving to five months of age, precluding some aspects of this study
evidence: Based on observation of mouse survival

claim: Knockout of Hdac2 in MSNs elicited a substantial transcriptional response, with ~11–12% of genes statistically significantly dysregulated (FDR adjusted p<0.05).
source: Strikingly, knockout of Hdac2 in MSNs elicited a substantial transcriptional response, roughly comparable in Htt+/+ or HttQ111/+ mice, with ~11–12% of genes statistically significantly dysregulated (FDR adjusted p<0.05) and being both up- and down-regulated in approximately equal proportion.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis results shown in Figure 2

claim: Hdac2 knockout resulted in both up- and down-regulation of genes in approximately equal proportion.
source: Strikingly, knockout of Hdac2 in MSNs elicited a substantial transcriptional response, roughly comparable in Htt+/+ or HttQ111/+ mice, with ~11–12% of genes statistically significantly dysregulated (FDR adjusted p<0.05) and being both up- and down-regulated in approximately equal proportion.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis results shown in Figure 2

claim: HttQ111/+ striata exhibited a large number of genes that were both up- and down-regulated.
source: In line with previous studies (Ament et al., 2017; Langfelder et al., 2016; Bragg et al., 2017), HttQ111/+ striata exhibited a large number of genes that were both up- and down-regulated, although only a moderate number reached statistical significance when accounting for multiple testing.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis results and citations to previous studies

claim: The transcriptional dysregulation mediated by the HttQ111 allele appeared to be somewhat muted in the Hdac2 knockout background.
source: Interestingly, the transcriptional dysregulation mediated by the HttQ111 allele appeared to be somewhat muted in the Hdac2 knockout background (Figure 2- compare contrasts 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison of differential expression results in contrasts 3 and 4 shown in Figure 2

claim: Analyses of exon-specific Hdac2 transcripts revealed marked depletion of reads mapping to exons 2, 3, and 4 in the Hdac2 KO mice.
source: Analyses of exon-specific Hdac2 transcripts revealed marked depletion of reads mapping to exons 2, 3, and 4 as well as the presence of exon 1-exon 5 splice junction reads in the Hdac2 ΚO mice, consistent with Cre-mediated deletion of exons 2–4 (Montgomery et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Analyses of transcript levels of other Hdac genes revealed a compensatory increase in Hdac1 transcripts in Hdac2 KO striata.
source: Analyses of transcript levels of other Hdac genes revealed a compensatory increase in Hdac1 transcripts in Hdac2 ΚO striata, consistent with western blots from the same mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but no major impact on the expression level of any other Hdac gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The HttQ111 allele did not alter expression of Hdac genes.
source: The HttQ111 allele did not alter expression of Hdac genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations that the HTT mutation does not influence HDAC expression in primary neurons, or in CAG140 knock-in mice, although expression of some HDACs was altered in R6/2 exon 1 transgenic mice (Hoshino et al., 2003; Quinti et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the full RNA-seq dataset revealed that the greatest variance between samples was attributable to Hdac2 genotype.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the full dataset revealed that the greatest variance between samples was attributable to Hdac2 genotype, with the second principal component largely separating males and females.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The second principal component of the RNA-seq PCA largely separated males and females.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the full dataset revealed that the greatest variance between samples was attributable to Hdac2 genotype, with the second principal component largely separating males and females.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: There was no clear distinction between RNA-seq samples based on Htt genotype in PCA.
source: There was no clear distinction between samples based on Htt genotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Global levels of striatal H3K9 and H4K12 acetylation revealed overall fairly subtle alterations that appeared to depend on age.
source: Global levels of striatal H3K9 and H4K12 acetylation, previously shown to be sensitive to HDAC2 levels in the brain (Guan et al., 2009), revealed overall fairly subtle alterations that appeared to depend on age (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citation to Guan et al., 2009

claim: The Hdac2 KO and HttQ111 mutations altered a number of shared processes and pathways.
source: These analyses revealed that the Hdac2 KO and HttQ111 mutations altered a number of shared processes and pathways.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Pathways related to cell adhesion, plasma membrane, calcium ion binding and morphine addiction were amongst the most significantly up-regulated in response to either the Hdac2 KO mutation or the HttQ111 allele.
source: For example, pathways related to cell adhesion, plasma membrane, calcium ion binding and morphine addiction were amongst the most significantly up-regulated in response to either the Hdac2 KO mutation (Figure 3, contrast 1) or the HttQ111 allele (Figure 3, contrast 3).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Pathways related to neuronal function were down-regulated in both Hdac2 KO striata and HttQ111/+ striata.
source: Broadly, pathways related to neuronal function were down-regulated in both in Hdac2 KO striata and HttQ111/+ striata, although the nature of these pathways was somewhat different, for example an enrichment for signaling pathways in HttQ111/+ striata and for pathways related to neuronal and synapse structure in the Hdac2 KO.
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: There was a highly significant overlap in the DEGs and enriched pathways due to the Hdac2 KO or the HttQ111 allele.
source: There was a highly significant overlap in the DEGs and enriched pathways due to the Hdac2 KO or the HttQ111 allele, largely reflecting overlaps in DEGs and enriched pathways altered in the same direction, i.e. up- or down-regulated in both conditions (statistical tests of enrichment were performed using one-sided Fisher exact tests – see Materials and methods, and results are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and statistical testing

claim: There were highly significant overlaps in the DEGs and enriched pathways altered in the same direction by Hdac2 KO in the presence and absence of the HttQ111 allele.
source: We also compared the effect of the Hdac2 KO in the presence and absence of the HttQ111 allele (Figure 3, contrasts 1 and 2). There were highly significant overlaps in the DEGs and enriched pathways altered in the same direction between two contrasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; pink highlighted cells).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: There were significant overlaps in DEGs and enriched pathways that were altered in the same direction by the HttQ111 allele in Hdac2 WT and KO conditions.
source: Again, there were significant overlaps in DEGs and enriched pathways that were altered in the same direction by the HttQ111 allele in Hdac2 WT and KO conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, blue highlighted cells).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: 152 genes dysregulated by HttQ111 had expression levels that did not differ significantly between Htt+/+ Hdac2 WT and HttQ111/+ Hdac2 KO striata.
source: 152 genes had expression levels that did not differ significantly between these two genotypes, of which 97 were down-regulated by HttQ111 and up-regulated by Hdac2 KO and 55 were up-regulated by HttQ111 and down-regulated by Hdac2 KO (Figure 4B, lower table, Source data 4).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and statistical testing

claim: These 152 genes represent ~12% of the total number of HttQ111-dysregulated genes (p<0.05).
source: These genes represent ~12% of the total number of HttQ111-dysregulated genes (p<0.05).
evidence: Calculated from differential expression analysis results

claim: Two genes (Ppp1r1b and Slc29a1) commonly dysregulated by HttQ111 in both studies had expression levels that did not differ between Htt+/+ Hdac2 WT and HttQ111/+ Hdac2 KO.
source: Two of these 29 genes (Ppp1r1b and Slc29a1) overlapped with the set of 152 genes whose expression level did not differ between Htt+/+ Hdac2 WT and HttQ111/+ Hdac2 KO (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: In the 29 commonly dysregulated genes, the relative impact of the HttQ111 allele was reduced in Hdac2 KO mice.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that in these 29 commonly dysregulated genes, the relative impact of the HttQ111 allele was reduced in Hdac2 KO mice. i.e. the difference in gene expression between HttQ111/+ and Htt+/+ is less in Hdac2 KO than in Hdac2 WT striata (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5

claim: Permutation showed a statistically significant enrichment for a reduced relative impact (absolute log2 fold-change) of the HttQ111 allele in the Hdac2 KO in the 29 commonly dysregulated genes (p<1e-5).
source: Permutation (Materials and methods) showed a statistically significant enrichment for a reduced relative impact (absolute log2 fold-change) of the HttQ111 allele in the Hdac2 KO in these 29 genes (p<1e-5).
evidence: Supported by permutation test analysis

claim: At 2.5 months of age, a subtle decrease in expansion index in Hdac2 KO striata was observed that was not statistically significant.
source: At 2.5 months of age, we observed a subtle decrease in expansion index in Hdac2 ΚO striata that was not statistically significant (Hdac2 WT: mean 5.76, 95% CI [4.64, 6.88]; Hdac2 KO: mean 5.29, 95% CI [4.23,6.35]; two-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.42).
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis shown in Figure 6 and statistical testing

claim: At 5 months of age the expansion index was significantly reduced in Hdac2 KO striata.
source: At 5 months of age the expansion index was significantly reduced in Hdac2 ΚO striata (Hdac2 WT: mean 15.22, 95% CI [14.16, 16.28]; Hdac2 ΚO: mean 12.69, 95% CI [10.91, 14.47]; 2-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.0094)
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis shown in Figure 6 and statistical testing

claim: At 10 months of age, a small reduction in expansion in Hdac2 KO striata was observed that did not reach statistical significance.
source: while at 10 months of age, we again observed a small reduction in expansion in Hdac2 ΚO striata; this was most apparent from the GeneMapper traces of closely CAG repeat-matched mice (panel A), though this did not reach statistical significance (Hdac2 WT: mean 21.55, 95% CI [19.62–23.48]; Hdac2 ΚO: mean 20.02, 95% CI [17.1–22.94]; two-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.26)
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis shown in Figure 6 and statistical testing

claim: Knockout of Hdac3 in MSNs decreased the expansion index in the striata of 5 month mice.
source: Knockout of Hdac3 in MSNs also decreased the expansion index in the striata of 5 month mice (Hdac3 WT: mean 13.94, 95% CI [12.81–15.07]; Hdac3 ΚO: mean 10.43, 95% CI [7.62–13.24]; two-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.0026).
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis shown in Figure 6 and statistical testing

claim: Expression of Cre recombinase itself did not impact CAG expansion.
source: Note that the expression of Cre recombinase itself did not impact CAG expansion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis in Cre control mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Neither Hdac2 KO nor Hdac3 KO resulted in any significant loss of MSNs as determined by the number of DARPP-32-positive cells.
source: Further, as neither Hdac2 ΚO nor Hdac3 ΚO resulted in any significant loss of MSNs as determined by the number of DARPP-32-positive cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), reduced striatal expansions cannot be readily explained by an altered cellular population biased toward stable alleles.
evidence: Supported by DARPP-32 immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Hdac2 and Hdac3 are moderate enhancers of CAG expansion in MSNs of HttQ111/+ mice.
source: Overall, our results support the conclusion that Hdac2 and Hdac3 are moderate enhancers of CAG expansion in MSNs of HttQ111/+ mice, with the impact of Hdac2 KO appearing to depend on the age of the mice.
evidence: Inferred from CAG expansion analysis results shown in Figure 6

claim: Msh3 mRNA levels were modestly decreased in HttQ111/+ Hdac2 KO striata relative to HttQ111/+ Hdac2 WT striata (nominal p<0.01; adjusted p=0.07).
source: Of these, only Msh3 mRNA levels were modestly decreased in HttQ111/+ Hdac2 ΚO striata relative to HttQ111/+ Hdac2 KO striata (nominal p<0.01; adjusted p=0.07) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B

claim: MSH3 protein levels were not reduced in Hdac2 KO striata.
source: However, MSH3 protein levels were not reduced in Hdac2 ΚO striata from these mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C, D

claim: The small molecule HDAC inhibitors SAHA, MS-275, and splitomicin stimulated CAG contractions in a cell-based assay.
source: In further support of a role for HDACs as modifiers of CAG instability we found that the small molecule HDAC inhibitors (Bradner et al., 2010), SAHA (suberanilohydroxamic acid), and MS-275, both of which share in common the potential inhibition of Zn2+-dependent Class I HDACs, and splitomicin, a weak inhibitor of NAD+ dependent Class III HDACs (Sirtuins) (Carafa et al., 2011), stimulated CAG contractions (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by cell-based contraction assay data shown in Figure 7B,C and citations

claim: The magnitude of effect of the HDAC inhibitors in the contraction assay was comparable to or exceeded that of various other genetic and pharmacological manipulations previously performed.
source: Remarkably, we note that the magnitude of effect of the HDAC inhibitors in this contraction assay was comparable to or exceeded that of the various other genetic and pharmacological manipulations we have previously performed (Lin and Wilson, 2009; Lin and Wilson, 2007; Lin and Wilson, 2012; Hubert et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison with previous studies cited

claim: HttQ111 mice exhibit both early (~2.5 months) diffusely immunostaining nuclear mutant huntingtin, detected with the anti-huntingtin antibody EM48 (or mAb5374), followed at ~6–12 months by the appearance of discreet intra-nuclear inclusions.
source: HttQ111 mice exhibit both early (~2.5 months) diffusely immunostaining nuclear mutant huntingtin, detected with the anti-huntingtin antibody EM48 (or mAb5374), followed at ~6–12 months by the appearance of discreet intra-nuclear inclusions (Wheeler et al., 2000; Wheeler et al., 2002; Lloret et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wheeler et al., 2000; Wheeler et al., 2002; Lloret et al., 2006

claim: Nuclear huntingtin pathology occurs selectively in MSNs in HttQ111 mice.
source: These cellular phenotypes, which occur selectively in MSNs in HttQ111 mice, are highly CAG repeat length-dependent and are modified by genes that alter somatic expansion (Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013

claim: Nuclear huntingtin pathology is highly CAG repeat length-dependent.
source: These cellular phenotypes, which occur selectively in MSNs in HttQ111 mice, are highly CAG repeat length-dependent and are modified by genes that alter somatic expansion (Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013

claim: Nuclear huntingtin pathology is modified by genes that alter somatic expansion.
source: These cellular phenotypes, which occur selectively in MSNs in HttQ111 mice, are highly CAG repeat length-dependent and are modified by genes that alter somatic expansion (Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kovalenko et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2013

claim: Hdac2 KO in MSNs reduced the intensity of diffusely immunostaining nuclear mutant huntingtin at 2.5 months.
source: Hdac2 ΚO in MSNs reduced the intensity of diffusely immunostaining nuclear mutant huntingtin at both 2.5 months (Hdac2 WT: mean 153.9, 95% CI [127.9, 179.9]; Hdac2 ΚO: mean 96.35, 95% CI [5.63, 187.1]; two-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.025)
evidence: Supported by mAb5374 immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 8 and statistical testing

claim: Hdac2 KO in MSNs reduced the intensity of diffusely immunostaining nuclear mutant huntingtin at 5 months of age, with a stronger impact than at 2.5 months.
source: and 5 months of age (Hdac2 WT: mean 226.8, 95% CI [159.9, 293.8]; Hdac2 ΚO: mean 120.9, 95% CI [77.34, 164.5]; two-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.0062), with a stronger impact at 5 months (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: Supported by mAb5374 immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 8 and statistical testing

claim: Diffuse nuclear huntingtin immunostaining was not altered by Cre expression alone.
source: Diffuse nuclear huntingtin immunostaining was not altered by Cre expression alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mAb5374 immunostaining quantification in Cre control mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: In 10-month mice, a decrease in the number of nuclei containing inclusions was observed in the low CAG group that did not reach statistical significance.
source: We observed a decrease in the number of nuclei containing inclusions in the low CAG group that did not reach statistical significance (Hdac2 WT: mean 8.76, 95% CI [−5.29, 22.81]; Hdac2 ΚO: mean 0.66, 95% CI [−7.74, 9.06]; 2-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.153)
evidence: Supported by nuclear inclusion quantification shown in Figure 8 and statistical testing

claim: In 10-month mice, a statistically significant decrease in the number of cells containing inclusions was observed in the high CAG group.
source: and a statistically significant decrease in the number of cells containing inclusions in the high CAG group (Hdac2 WT: mean 37.8, 95% CI [21.26, 54.31]; Hdac2 ΚO: mean 23.44, 95% CI [16.58, 30.31]; 2-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.0261).
evidence: Supported by nuclear inclusion quantification shown in Figure 8 and statistical testing

claim: In the 5-month Hdac3 KO cohort, a non-statistically significant trend towards decreased diffuse nuclear mutant huntingtin was observed.
source: In the 5-month Hdac3 KO cohort, we observed a non-statistically significant trend towards decreased diffuse nuclear mutant huntingtin in a small number of immunostained 5-month Hdac3 ΚO striata (Hdac3 WT: mean 234, 95% CI [91.13, 376.9]; Hdac3 ΚO: mean 181.2, 95% CI [72.92, 289.5]; two-tailed unpaired t-test p=0.21). (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by mAb5374 immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 8C and statistical testing

claim: There was a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.87, p=0.0011) between mAb5374 intensity and expansion index in the 5-month Hdac2 KO cohort.
source: There was a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.87, p=0.0011) between mAb5374 intensity and expansion index (Figure 8D), consistent with somatic CAG expansion as a modifier of this cellular phenotype.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8D

claim: Hdac2 KO decreased total huntingtin mRNA levels in Htt+/+ striata by 5.9% (nominal p=0.06; adjusted p=0.25).
source: In the RNA-seq data, Hdac2 KO decreased total huntingtin mRNA levels in Htt+/+ striata by 5.9% (nominal p=0.06; adjusted p=0.25)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Hdac2 KO decreased total huntingtin mRNA levels in HttQ111/+ striata by 11% (nominal p<0.001; adjusted p<0.05).
source: and in HttQ111/+ striata by 11% (nominal p<0.001; adjusted p<0.05) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Western blot analyses did not provide evidence for an impact of Hdac2 KO on steady state levels of wild-type or mutant huntingtin protein.
source: However, western blot analyses on the contralateral striata from a subset of the mice used for RNA-seq did not provide evidence for an impact of Hdac2 KO on steady state levels of wild-type or mutant huntingtin protein (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: Exon1-intron1-spanning transcripts were identified in HttQ111/+ striata.
source: In support of previous data (Sathasivam et al., 2013), we identified exon1-intron1-spanning transcripts in HttQ111/+ striata.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and citation to Sathasivam et al., 2013

claim: Hdac2 KO had no impact on the number of exon1-intron1-spanning transcripts.
source: However, Hdac2 KO had no impact on the number of these sequence reads (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B

claim: MSN-specific knockout of Hdac2 reversed the transcriptional dysregulation of a subset of genes.
source: Our results show that MSN-specific knockout of Hdac2 reversed the transcriptional dysregulation of a subset of genes and resulted in a moderate reduction in somatic CAG expansion and nuclear huntingtin pathology.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis, CAG expansion analysis, and nuclear huntingtin immunostaining quantification

claim: MSN-specific knockout of Hdac2 resulted in a moderate reduction in somatic CAG expansion.
source: Our results show that MSN-specific knockout of Hdac2 reversed the transcriptional dysregulation of a subset of genes and resulted in a moderate reduction in somatic CAG expansion and nuclear huntingtin pathology.
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: MSN-specific knockout of Hdac2 resulted in a moderate reduction in nuclear huntingtin pathology.
source: Our results show that MSN-specific knockout of Hdac2 reversed the transcriptional dysregulation of a subset of genes and resulted in a moderate reduction in somatic CAG expansion and nuclear huntingtin pathology.
evidence: Supported by nuclear huntingtin immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 8

claim: MSN-specific knockout of Hdac3 resulted in a comparable reduction in somatic CAG expansion to the Hdac2 knockout.
source: MSN-specific knockout of Hdac3 resulted in a comparable reduction in somatic CAG expansion to the Hdac2 knockout.
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: HDAC1 is unable to compensate for the lack of HDAC2 in MSNs, providing evidence for a specific role of HDAC2 in MSNs.
source: Our data reveal that, despite its up-regulation, HDAC1 is unable to compensate for the lack of HDAC2 in MSNs, providing evidence for a specific role of HDAC2 in MSNs and supporting distinct functions of HDAC1 and HDAC2 in adult neurons (Guan et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from substantial transcriptional dysregulation despite HDAC1 upregulation, supported by citations

claim: The expression level of approximately 12% of genes dysregulated by the HttQ111 allele was normalized by the Hdac2 KO to levels present in wild-type mice.
source: The expression level of approximately 12% of genes dysregulated by the HttQ111 allele was normalized by the Hdac2 KO to levels present in wild-type mice.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: A large proportion (~24%) of genes dysregulated by the HttQ111 allele was further dysregulated in the same direction by the Hdac2 KO.
source: Indeed, a large proportion (~24%) of genes dysregulated by the HttQ111 allele was further dysregulated in the same direction by the Hdac2 KO.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Hdac2 KO lessened the relative impact of the HttQ111 allele in a set of the most significantly HttQ111-dysregulated genes, regardless of the absolute gene expression change elicited by the Hdac2 KO.
source: In addition, and apparent in a set of the most significantly HttQ111-dysregulated genes, Hdac2 KO lessens the relative impact of the HttQ111 mutation, regardless of the absolute effect of the Hdac2 KO on the level of gene expression.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5 and permutation testing

claim: The genetic interaction between Hdac2 KO and HttQ111 indicates a functional relationship between these two mutations that may in part reflect a role of huntingtin in regulating the REST-containing transcriptional repressor complex that includes HDAC2.
source: This genetic interaction indicates a functional relationship between these two mutations that may in part reflect a role of huntingtin in regulating the REST-containing transcriptional repressor complex that includes HDAC2 (Buckley et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction data and supported by citation to Buckley et al., 2010

claim: HDAC inhibitors with activity against HDAC2 would have the potential to reverse some of the early transcriptional changes elicited by an expanded CAG mutation.
source: Our data indicate that HDAC inhibitors with activity against HDAC2 would have the potential to reverse some of the early transcriptional changes elicited by an expanded CAG mutation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Hdac2 KO reversed a subset of HttQ111-dysregulated genes

claim: The results indicate a complex relationship between the expanded CAG repeat mutation and Hdac2, with potential implications for therapies directed at HDAC2 inhibition.
source: However, our results also indicate a complex relationship between the expanded CAG repeat mutation and Hdac2, with potential implications for therapies directed at HDAC2 inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Hdac2 KO both reversed and exacerbated gene dysregulation by HttQ111

claim: Hdac2 and Hdac3 are enhancers of CAG expansion in MSNs.
source: We demonstrate here that Hdac2 and Hdac3 are enhancers of CAG expansion in MSNs.
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis showing reduced expansion in knockout mice

claim: Neither knockout of Hdac2 nor Hdac3 had a large impact on CAG expansion, in contrast to a number of MMR genes that are fundamental drivers of this process and whose knockouts eliminate expansion.
source: It is important to note that neither knockout of Hdac2 nor Hdac3 had a large impact on CAG expansion, in contrast to a number of MMR genes that are fundamental drivers of this process and whose knockouts eliminate expansion (Wheeler et al., 2003; Dragileva et al., 2009; Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison of CAG expansion effects with previous studies cited

claim: The results are consistent with those of Suelves et al. in which treatment of HttQ111 mice with HDAC inhibitor RGFP966 resulted in a slight reduction in striatal CAG expansion.
source: Our results are consistent with those of Suelves et al. in which treatment of HttQ111 mice with HDAC inhibitor RGFP966, resulted in a slight reduction in striatal CAG expansion (Suelves et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with previous study cited

claim: HDAC3 and HDAC5 enhanced CAG expansion in a selectable human astrocyte cell-based assay, whereas HDAC9 suppressed expansions.
source: HDAC3 and HDAC5 enhanced CAG expansion in a selectable human astrocyte cell-based assay, whereas HDAC9 suppressed expansions (Debacker et al., 2012; Gannon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Debacker et al., 2012 and Gannon et al., 2012

claim: A role for HDAC2 was not implicated in the human astrocyte cell-based assay, based on differential effects of HDAC inhibitors with selectivity towards HDACs 1 and 2 or HDAC3.
source: A role for HDAC2 was not implicated in this system, based on differential effects of HDAC inhibitors with selectivity towards HDACs 1 and 2 or HDAC3 (Debacker et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Debacker et al., 2012

claim: It is possible that Hdac2 or Hdac3 modify CAG instability by altering chromatin structure close to the CAG repeat tract.
source: Therefore, it is possible that Hdac2 or Hdac3 modify CAG instability by altering chromatin structure close to the CAG repeat tract.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on known roles of HDAC2 and HDAC3

claim: It is possible that changes in acetylation of DNA repair proteins could lead to their altered activity.
source: However, it is possible that changes in acetylation of DNA repair proteins could lead to their altered activity (Chatterjee et al., 2012; Choudhary et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014; Radhakrishnan et al., 2015; Piekna-Przybylska et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations

claim: Hdac2 knockout modifies nuclear intensity and inclusion phenotypes in HttQ111 mice at least in part as a consequence of reduced CAG expansion in MSNs.
source: We suggest that Hdac2 knockout modifies nuclear intensity and inclusion phenotypes in HttQ111 mice at least in part as a consequence of reduced CAG expansion in MSNs.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between expansion index and nuclear huntingtin intensity

claim: The modest reduction in CAG expansion caused by the Hdac2 knockout is unlikely to explain the reversal of transcriptional dysregulation elicited by the HttQ111 allele.
source: In contrast, the modest reduction in CAG expansion caused by the Hdac2 knockout is unlikely to explain the reversal of transcriptional dysregulation elicited by the HttQ111 allele, in which gene expression levels that can be distinguished between wild-type and HttQ111/+ mice appear effectively normalized to wild-type in HttQ111/+ mice harboring the Hdac2 knockout mutation.
evidence: Inferred from the magnitude of transcriptional changes relative to the modest reduction in CAG expansion

claim: Hdac2 and Hdac3 are modifiers of different aspects of the HD pathogenic process in MSNs.
source: In summary, we have tested whether Hdac2 and Hdac3 are modifiers of different aspects of the HD pathogenic process in MSNs that are both inherently prone to CAG repeat expansion and specifically vulnerable in the disease process.
evidence: Supported by data showing effects on CAG expansion, transcription, and nuclear pathology

claim: The results of this study indicate moderate effects of Hdac2 and Hdac3 on CAG expansion, which in humans drives the rate of disease onset.
source: The results of this study indicate moderate effects of these genes on CAG expansion, which in humans drives the rate of disease onset, and for Hdac2, on downstream molecular and cellular phenotypes that may be important in cellular toxicity mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by CAG expansion analysis and knowledge of CAG expansion's role in disease onset

claim: Hdac2 has effects on downstream molecular and cellular phenotypes that may be important in cellular toxicity mechanisms.
source: The results of this study indicate moderate effects of these genes on CAG expansion, which in humans drives the rate of disease onset, and for Hdac2, on downstream molecular and cellular phenotypes that may be important in cellular toxicity mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by transcriptional and nuclear pathology data
